overview:
South Sudan became the world's newest country in 2011, when it separated from Sudan after decades of war. It is landlocked in east-central Africa, bordered by Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic, and covers about 620,000 km², roughly the size of France. The capital is Juba, a river port on the White Nile.

Around 11 million people live in South Sudan, belonging to more than sixty ethnic groups; the Dinka and Nuer are the largest. English is the official language, while a simplified form called Juba Arabic serves as a common tongue in markets, and Dinka, Nuer and Zande are spoken at home. Most people are Christian or follow traditional beliefs. Cattle stand at the center of life, wealth and ceremony across much of the country. South Sudan is a republic with plentiful oil but few paved roads outside the capital, and it remains one of the world's least developed countries.
landAndNature: The White Nile flows north through the heart of the country and spreads into the Sudd, one of the largest wetlands on Earth, a maze of papyrus, reeds and floating islands that can double in size during the rains and once blocked boats from sailing upriver. Around it stretch grassy plains and woodland, and the Imatong Mountains rise near the Ugandan border to about 3,187 meters at Mount Kinyeti. South Sudan hosts one of the greatest animal migrations left on the planet: well over a million white-eared kob, tiang and gazelle sweep across the Boma and Badingilo plains in long columns, followed by lions and hyenas. Elephants, giraffes and shoebill storks live here too.
peopleAndCulture: Cattle shape daily life for Dinka, Nuer and Mundari herders, who name favorite bulls, compose songs about them and dust them with ash to keep off flies. Young people know their cattle camp the way others know a hometown. Sorghum and millet are ground into porridge and eaten with stews of okra, beans, peanuts or fish from the Nile. Communities gather for wrestling matches, a serious sport with drums, chanting and champions known across whole regions. Dances mark weddings and harvests. South Sudanese are famously tall, and several have become star basketball players abroad; the national team reached the Olympics in 2024.
history: Nilotic peoples, including the Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk, have herded cattle in these grasslands for many centuries. Egyptian and Ottoman expeditions pushed up the Nile in the 1800s, raiding for slaves and ivory, and Britain later governed the south separately from the Arabic-speaking north within Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. When Sudan became independent in 1956, southerners feared domination, and two long civil wars followed, from 1955 to 1972 and from 1983 to 2005, killing millions and forcing many more from their homes. A peace deal in 2005 promised a vote, and in 2011 almost 99 percent of southerners chose separation. Independence came on July 9, 2011, but a power struggle brought civil war from 2013 to 2018, and recovery has been slow.
funFacts: South Sudan is the world's newest widely recognized country, independent since July 9, 2011.
The Sudd wetland is so vast that its papyrus mazes once made the upper Nile nearly impossible to navigate.
More than a million antelope migrate across South Sudan's plains, a spectacle that rivals the Serengeti's wildebeest.
Mundari herders sleep beside their cattle and rub themselves with ash, which dries white and keeps insects away.
South Sudan's basketball team qualified for the Olympics in 2024, only thirteen years after the country was founded.
